Tentative Rulings
February 25, 2026
Department S-17
Judge Joseph Ortiz
______________________________________________________________________
Tentative Rulings for Department S-17 are posted on the court’s website (https://www.sb-
court.org/divisions/civil/civil-tentative-rulings) at 3:00 p.m. or at 7:00 p.m. the court day before
the hearing. If no tentative ruling is posted at 3:00 p.m., please check again after 7:00 p.m.
Unless you wish to submit on the tentative ruling, you must appear for the hearing either in
person, CourtCall (888-882-6878 or www.courtcall.com), or by ZOOM. Failure to appear is
deemed a waiver of oral argument. If you wish to submit to the tentative, please call the
Judicial Assistant at (909) 708-8715 in advance of the hearing. If all parties submit on a
tentative ruling, it will become final. The tentative ruling may seek input on particular issues
and direct appearance. If so directed, attendance at the hearing is mandatory. The party
prevailing on a motion or other hearing shall serve written notice of the court’s ruling unless all
parties waive notice of the ruling.
ATTENTION: Since January 9, 2023, the court no longer provides an official Court Reporter to
transcribe proceedings. Parties who wish to have a transcript must retain their own private
reporter and must submit a “Stipulation and Order to Use Certified Shorthand Reporter.”
Parties who do not retain their own reporter have waived the right to one.
UNLESS OTHERWISE NOTED, THE PREVAILING PARTY IS TO GIVE NOTICE OF THE RULING.

16. Singh v. Velocity Truck Centers, Case No. CIVSB2433611
Defendant’s Motion to Dismiss
2/25/26, 9:00 a.m., Dept. S-17
The Court would GRANT this unopposed motion. In this case, on October 14, 2025, the Court
sustained Defendant’s demurrer but granted twenty days’ leave to amend. Despite the grant of
leave, Plaintiff failed to file an amended complaint within the twenty days. As such, Defendant
filed this instant motion on November 13, 2025, seeking dismissal pursuant Code of Civil
Procedure section 581(f)(2). To date no amended complaint has been filed nor has any
opposition to the instant motion been presented.
*** *** ***
17. Stanley, et al, v. Lake Chalet Homeowners Association, et al, Case No. CIVSB2320918
Stanley Plaintiffs’ Motion for Judgment on the Pleadings as to the Answer
2/25/26, 9:00 a.m., Dept. S-17
Tentative Rulings
The Court would DENY the motion, in part, as to the first, third, fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth,
ninth, tenth, sixteenth, seventeenth, eighteenth, nineteenth, twenty-first, twenty-second,
twenty-third, twenty-fourth, twenty-fifth, and twenty-sixth affirmative defenses.
The Court would GRANT, in part, with thirty (30) days’ leave to amend, as to the second, fourth,
eleventh, twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and twenty-seventh affirmative defenses.
The Court would also GRANT, in part, as to the twentieth affirmative defense without leave
amend, as Defendants have withdrawn the reservation of rights to add more defenses in their
Asnwer.
Case Summary
In essence, this is a breach of fiduciary duty case. Plaintiffs own one unit of a triplex that is
subject to the Covenants, Conditions, and Restrictions (CC&Rs) of Defendant Lake Chalet
Homeowners Association (HOA). Plaintiffs assert that Defendant HOA violated the CC&Rs and
relevant Bylaws by failing to maintain and repair common areas; not maintaining proper
financial records; allowing Defendants Prine to make unilateral decisions concerning the
development without proper meetings or voting; and permitting short term rentals in violation
2
of the CC&Rs and City regulations and ordinances. As such, Plaintiffs filed suit on September 8,
2023. The operative First Amended Complaint (FAC) asserts causes for (1) breach of the HOA
governing documents; (2) breach of fiduciary duty; (3) negligence; (4) nuisance; (5) violation of
open meeting act; (6) failure to permit inspection of records; and (7) declaratory relief.
On October 30, 2023, the Prine Defendants filed a Cross-Complaint against Plaintiffs (Cross-
Defendants). They filed a First Amended Cross-Complaint (FACC) against Plaintiffs on November
6, 2023, alleging causes for (1) breach of the CC&Rs; (2) nuisance; (3) interference with
contractual relations; and (4) declaratory relief. On November 20, 2023, the HOA Defendant
also filed a Cross-Complaint against Plaintiffs (Cross-Defendants), asserting causes for (1)
breach of the CC&Rs; (2) nuisance; and (3) declaratory relief. And, on November 20, 2023, the
HOA filed a Cross-Complaint against Cross-Defendants Stanley for (1) breach of equitable
servitude/ CC&Rs; (2) nuisance; and (3) declaratory relief.
Statement of Law
If the moving party is a plaintiff, the motion for judgment on the pleadings (JOP) is limited to
that the complaint states facts sufficient to constitute a cause or causes of action against the
defendant and the answer does not state facts sufficient to constitute a defense to the
complaint. (Code Civ. Proc., § 438(c)(1)(A).) The motion may be made to the entire answer or as
to any of the affirmative defenses stated therein. (Code Civ. Proc., § 438(c)(2)(B).)
Analysis
Defendants’ joint Answer asserts a general denial and twenty-seven affirmative defenses.
Plaintiffs move for JOP contending that all of Defendants’ affirmative defenses only plead legal
theories when such defenses must be “averred as carefully and with as much detail as the
facts” alleged in the complaint. (Department of Finance v. City of Merced (2019) 33 Cal.App.5th
286, 294.) Plaintiffs challenge all the affirmative defenses.
Waived arguments: Plaintiffs raise no specific argument as to the first affirmative defense for
failure to state a cause of action, seventh affirmative defense for comparative negligence,
eighth affirmative defense for consent, sixteenth affirmative defense for apportionment,
seventeenth affirmative defense for comparative indemnity, twenty-second affirmative defense
for offset, and twenty-sixth affirmative defense for accord and satisfaction. As Plaintiffs failed
to support their motion against these affirmative defenses “with reasoned argument and
citations to authority, we treat the point[s] as waived.” (Badie v. Bank of America (1998) 67
Cal.App.4th 779, 784-785.)
Defenses that are denials: It is undisputed that many of the contested affirmative defenses are,
in fact, denials. These include, but are not limited to, the third defense for actions consistent
with governing documents, the fifth defense for lack of notice, and others. Plaintiffs cite State
Farm Mutual Auto Insurance Company for support, reasoning that where an allegation is
“directed to an essential element of plaintiff’s cause of action, it does not constitute new
3
matter and need not be specifically alleged.” (State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins. Co. v. Superior Court
(1991) 228 Cal.App.3d 721, 726.) However, Plaintiffs miss the point. Holding a matter need not
be alleged does not lead to the conclusion that it may not be alleged.
The State Farm case answered whether it was proper for the trial court to exclude all evidence
of State Farm’s advice of counsel defense to a claim of insurance bad faith because it had failed
to specifically plead advice of counsel. (State Farm Mut. Auto. Ins., supra, 228 Cal.App.3d at pp.
723-724.) The Court of Appeal concluded “the defense of reliance on advice of counsel to a
claim of insurance bad faith may be shown under a general denial of the complaint and
accordingly grant[ed] the [writ of mandate to vacate the order].” (Id., at p. 724.) In other words,
the defense was implicit in the denial and need not have been specifically pleaded. There is,
however, no prohibition on such affirmative defenses. Further still, as denials that merely
contradict essential allegations, there is no need to plead further facts in support of them.
Thus, the Court would deny the motion as to third, fifth, sixth, ninth, tenth, eighteenth,
nineteenth, twenty-first, twenty-third, twenty-fourth, and twenty-fifth affirmative defenses.
Defenses lacking sufficient factual allegations:1 Plaintiffs rely on Hayward Lumber & Inv. Co. v.
Construction Products Corp. (1953) 117 Cal.App.2d 221, 228, which stated “[t]he party relying
upon an equitable defense must plead it with some particularity.” Plaintiffs are correct that
certain affirmative defenses are creatures of equity. (See, e.g., Mission Housing Development
Co. v. City & County of San Francisco (1997) 59 Cal.App.4th 55, 75 [waiver]; Brownrigg v. De
Frees (1925) 196 Cal.534, 539 [laches]; Piscioneri v. City of Ontario (2002) 95 Cal.App.4th 1037,
1053 [unclean hands].) Therefore, Plaintiffs argue the Defendants equitable defenses do not
meet the heightened pleading standard. The Court largely agrees. The Court would grant as to
eleventh, thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth affirmative defenses because they are new
equitable matters, but the Court would grant leave to amend.
Similarly, the Court would grant with leave to amend as to the second (business judgment) and
fourth (judicial deference) defenses. Plaintiffs contend that these defenses cannot apply to this
dispute because these principles cannot apply to a homeowners’ association’s decision to
violate the Civil Code and it is not an excuse for a homeowners’ association’s decision to violate
a municipal regulation. Notably, on a motion for JOP, the challenge is only to the legal
sufficiency of the pleadings, not their veracity. Thus, it is of no concern whether Defendants can
prove their affirmative defenses. (Lance Camper Manufacturing Corp. v. Republic Indemnity Co.
(1996) 44 Cal.App.4th 194, 198.)
Defendants nonetheless need to provide factual allegations in support of these affirmative
defenses, not only legal conclusions. (Ekstrom v. Marquesa at Monarch Beach Homeowners
1 Defendants are silent as to the twenty-seventh affirmative defense and therefore concede the argument.
(DuPont Merck Pharmaceutical Co. v. Superior Court (2000) 78 Cal.App.4th 562, 566 [“By failing to argue the
contrary, plaintiffs concede this issue.”]; See Pacifica First National, Inc. v. Abekasis (2021) 50 Cal.App.5th 654, 657
[Not returning to a topic on reply, “is a concession.”].)
4
Assn. (2008) 168 Cal.App.4th 1111, 1123 [“Just as the corporate business judgment rule, which
is a rule of judicial deference to good faith management decisions of corporate boards, is a
defense [citation], so too is the rule of judicial deference to decisions of homeowner
association boards articulated in Lamden.”].) Under the second affirmative defense, Defendants
state they acted in accordance with the business judgment rule as set forth in Lambden and
Corporations Code section 7230, et seq. Under the fourth affirmative defense, Defendants state
their decisions were made in good faith following a reasonable investigation and based upon
their assessment of the best interests of the association and its members. While the framework
is there, Defendants should set forth supporting facts.
The twentieth affirmative defense is withdrawn: Plaintiffs correctly state that Defendants
cannot reserve the right to add more defenses at will, which is what the twentieth affirmative
defense purports to do. Defendants, in their opposition, agree and withdraw it. Thus, the Court
would grant without leave to amend as to this “defense”. If Defendants later discovery
information to support the addition of other affirmative defenses, they may seek leave of the
court to amend the answer.
